Chapter One: Rethinking Time—The 168-Hour Perspective
Have you ever felt like time’s always slipping through your fingers? Maybe you’ve caught yourself saying, “There just aren’t enough hours in the day”—whether it’s work, family, or just finding a little space for yourself. But here’s a surprising truth: no matter who you are or where you come from, every single one of us gets the exact same weekly gift—168 hours.
When you look at it that way, it can really change how you think about your time. Instead of feeling trapped by those jam-packed days, imagine zooming out and seeing your whole week laid out in front of you. Suddenly, things don’t feel quite so packed. Picture your week like a giant blank grid, with 168 little squares, each one just waiting for you to decide how to fill it.
The beauty of this 168-hour framework is how it lets you step back from rushing through day after day. You get to see the bigger picture. And often, when you do this, that nagging feeling of not having enough time starts to fade. Take someone with a typical 40-hour work week who sleeps eight hours a night—believe it or not, there are still more than 70 hours left over.
That realization can feel both freeing and a little bit daunting. It nudges you to question the old story that life’s just too crowded for anything meaningful.
So, where do you even begin? It all starts with getting honest about how you actually spend your hours. Most of us overestimate how much time goes to things like work or chores, and totally underestimate how much slips away on autopilot. Our minds love to focus on those super-busy moments, which can trick us into thinking we’re always rushed.
But when you start tracking your time—maybe with a notebook, a simple spreadsheet, or an app—suddenly, little patterns pop up. Those tiny pockets of time you never noticed before? They add up. For example, a parent feeling stretched thin by work and family might discover, after adding everything up, that there are still a few hours each day that haven’t been claimed by anyone or anything.
And here’s the thing: this isn’t about cramming more productivity into every single minute. It’s about shining a light on where your time really goes. Once you map out your full 168 hours, you’ll start to see exactly where you’re making choices—sometimes without even realizing it.
Think of it like turning on a light in a messy room. Suddenly, you can see what’s actually there, and you get to decide what stays and what needs to change.
If you’re curious to try this out, let’s talk about a few gentle guidelines for your first time audit:
First, try to record what you’re doing in real time, or as close as you can—that way your memory doesn’t play tricks on you. Next, use big categories like work, sleep, family, or leisure, but jot down some details when it makes sense. And at the end of the week, take a few minutes to review what you’ve tracked. Look for any surprises or patterns that jump out.
Most people find that the feeling of “not enough time” has less to do with not having enough hours, and more to do with how those hours are spread out.
The 168-hour perspective invites you to shift from just reacting to what time throws at you… to actually shaping your week. It’s kind of like the difference between drifting down a river and picking up the oars, steering your own course.
